beats.got: nothing new

beats.trigger: Hire three agents to search. Three more to decide.
beats.got: nothing new. 'Hire' is a loose word for software, and there's no cost attached.

beats.got: The last bullet is the only one about whether it pays off. The rest is building things.

beats.trigger: What do you expect will get lost between them?

beats.trigger: The agent writes the exact message first and sends only after approval.
beats.got: The agent proposes and a human approves before anything leaves the building. That is a control I could take to the board.

beats.trigger: Push back hard when the first answer restates the problem.
beats.got: I'm to have the AI name the one problem that matters. Rumelt is a consultant reference, and I can't tell if the answer will be any good.

beats.trigger: Separate sessions share files, each with its own context and connectors.
beats.got: Four windows and five prompts over about 28 minutes. I see no cost or payback figure for any of it.

beats.trigger: You can't yet tell if it is right; that is expected.

beats.trigger: Your team will ask: *when do I split, and how?*
beats.got: There is a decision rule coming, so I'm paying attention.

beats.trigger: A hundred tiny agents cost more to coordinate than they save.
beats.got: Too many agents cost more than they save. That's the first cost statement in the module, though there's no number.

beats.trigger: If one agent can produce what you need, use one.
beats.got: The default is the cheap option, and you add complexity only when it's justified. That is how I run a budget.

beats.trigger: A legal-policy agent shouldn't have customer-data access.
beats.got: Three tests for splitting, and one of them is access separation. I understand that, and it is a GDPR and audit point.

beats.trigger: Split for a reason, not because "three is more thorough"
beats.got: More of something is not more quality. They say it themselves, which earns some trust.

beats.trigger: The stances bring the variety. The frame brings the choice.
beats.got: Without a decision framework the output is a summary and nobody has chosen. Fair, but I don't know how I'd check the choice.

beats.trigger: Could one prompt produce the same quality of output?
beats.got: A one-question test before spending on more agents.

beats.trigger: **Helper agents in one session (the Phase 2 move).**
beats.got: Two ways to set it up, windows or helpers. It is technical and I would leave it to IT.

beats.trigger: Other agents are part of the tool surface: one agent can call a different stance, source zone, or working style.
beats.got: nothing new

beats.trigger: A retriever finds two numbers and the curator keeps one.

beats.trigger: A whole module showed multi-agent works. Don't apply it to everything.
beats.got: They tell me not to over-apply what they just taught. That is rare, and I respect it.

beats.got: Agents fail, sometimes confidently. At least that's honest.

beats.trigger: This prompt is long. Make your own variant.
beats.got: A long prompt to find out why it broke. I'm not the one who would run it.

beats.trigger: move the risky step from "do" to "propose."

beats.trigger: Keep the unease about the synthesized briefing as an open question. Do not fix it today.

beats.got: nothing new

beats.got: A summary I can repeat: split only for access, dialect or stance.

beats.got: nothing new. More reading.

beats.trigger: Agents add non-deterministic behaviour, prompt injection (direct, or inside retrieved text) and emergent capability you can only bound.
beats.got: The module names the risk list: prompt injection, secrets in context, a skill supply chain. I'd want these in IT's review.

beats.trigger: An agent that works across connected systems has access to those systems.
beats.got: The question is what the worst case is, which is how I assess any risk. It should have come first.

beats.trigger: You're close to an agent system that cracks your crux.
beats.got: They say I'm close to cracking my crux. I have no evidence of that, only a promise.

take_homes: Start with one agent. Split only for a reason, which is access, dialect or stance. Extra agents are extra cost.
Handoffs between agents lose information, such as the second number, and nothing in the module checks whether the final briefing is true.
Where it matters, the agent proposes and a person approves. That is the control I would require for finance.

monday.move: Nothing on agents. I'll ask IT and legal what is approved for finance data, and ask my controller what one agent on the month-end variance commentary would cost per month and who checks the output.
monday.stop_condition: Stop if nobody can give me a monthly cost or a named checker
monday.blocker: IT has not approved the tool for finance data, and I have no cost figure.

misconception.why: I heard 'don't split by default', 'more agents is not more rigour' and 'does not check whether the briefing is true'. They support my caution but not the idea that AI is a capability the organisation builds. I still see a licence and a cost to defend. The module gave me no cost, payback or adoption figure, so my view of AI as something you buy is unchanged.

one_line: Honest about where it breaks and 'start with one agent' is sound, but I came out with no cost figure and the AI marks its own homework.
